analysis.one_liner: Blocks a federal rule that would cut truck drivers' hours to prevent fatigue crashes.
analysis.headline: A bill with 46 cosponsors that would have blocked a truck driver fatigue-safety rule died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In May 2000, the federal truck safety agency proposed a rule rewriting how many hours truck drivers may work and drive, aimed at reducing crashes caused by tired drivers. This bill would have prohibited the Transportation Secretary and the truck safety agency from finalizing, carrying out, or enforcing that rule, and would have forced any future final rule to sit for 180 days before taking effect. The bill never got past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Trucking companies and freight operators, who would avoid the cost of reworking driver schedules and keep maximum flexibility in how long drivers stay on duty.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Transportation Secretary and the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration from taking any action or using any funds to finalize, implement, or enforce the May 2000 proposed 'Hours of Service of Drivers' rule.
Allows the agency to continue earlier stages of the rulemaking — including a new proposed rule — but bars it from adopting a final rule.
Adds a 180-day waiting period after any final rule is sent to Congress before it can take effect, extending the status quo further.

analysis.who_pays: Truck drivers, who would keep working under old, longer-hours rules linked to driver fatigue, and everyone sharing the road with heavy trucks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Truck drivers and everyone on the road

drawbacks.text: The bill's core effect is to stop or delay a safety rule aimed at reducing crashes caused by exhausted truck drivers, leaving drivers and the public without those protections for at least the life of the bill.

Supporters' strongest good-faith case: the proposed rule imposed significant rework costs on carriers and set uniform schedules that industry argued would not fit all operations or clearly reduce fatigue; a blanket prohibition, however, removes the rule even where its safety case was strong, rather than tailoring it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs to trucking companies of adjusting driver schedules are real, but the bill's approach — an outright prohibition on finishing a fatigue-safety rule plus a built-in 180-day delay for any future version — weighs in favor of scheduling flexibility over driver and public safety. It is hard to justify blocking an agency rulemaking outright rather than amending the rule.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's highways subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lee Terry introduced the bill on March 13, 2001, with the goal of prohibiting the Transportation Secretary and the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration from finalizing or enforcing the May 2000 proposed hours-of-service rule.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Highways and Transit.
It gathered 46 cosponsors — 45 Republicans and 1 Democrat — but no further action of any kind was taken before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking companies, which continued operating under the old hours rules for the rest of the Congress since the fatigue rule was never finalized anyway, and never faced this bill's added delays. Drivers and the public gained nothing, but were spared the bill's outright prohibition on the rule.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trucking companies, under the old rules

for.name: Rep. Lee Terry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the May 2000 truck driver hours-of-service rule.

for.name: American Trucking Associations and other motor carrier groups
for.what_they_did: Opposed the 2000 hours-of-service rule and backed efforts in Congress to block it.

against.name: Rep. Don Young
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action; it sat at subcommittee referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Highway and driver safety advocates
against.role: Safety groups supporting the fatigue rule
against.what_they_did: Supported finalizing the hours-of-service rule and opposed congressional attempts to block it.

sides.party_line_note: 46 of the 47 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the single Democratic cosponsor made the bill nearly one-sided by party, and it died in a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have blocked a rule limiting how long drivers can work, saving carriers the cost of reworking schedules and preserving maximum use of driver hours. The industry's gain comes at the cost of driver rest and reduced fatigue-related crash risk for the public.
Truck drivers would remain under the older, longer-hours rules, keeping more time on duty but facing more fatigue — their interest in shorter hours runs alongside public road safety.
